metadata.title: Translation invariant pure state on $\otimes_{\IZ}\!M_d(\IC)$ and Haag duality

extraction_notes.note: The paper has no \label/\ref; every cross-reference is in words, and numbering is inconsistent ("Theorem 2.4/3.4/3.5" mean Propositions 2.4/3.4/3.5; "Theorem 2.6 (a)" in the proof of Theorem 1.1 must mean Theorem 3.6(a)). All uses edges were added by hand to the intended nodes.
Marked origin external because the paper attributes them to Popescu/BJKW ("we recall", "easy adaptations of results proved in [BJKW]") although it gives its own proofs; the proofs are origin paper.
open_problem rather than problem: questions the paper raises in prose and then answers (fully or for pure states) with Theorem 1.1/3.6, recorded by resolves edges.

Repeated statements kept once: BJKW Lemma 7.4 (intro copy dropped for Proposition 2.6), the Section 3 repeat of the dual Popescu elements and KMS relations (equation (29) kept as an equation node), the intro sketch of Popescu dilation (Theorem 2.1 kept), and the three mentions of the type-I/III dichotomy. Weak isomorphism and other historical discussion not used later were not extracted.

The key arguments are page-long transfinite constructions (strict partial orders on quasi-equivalent representations plus Hausdorff maximality); the run-in conditions (C1)-(C3), (C3'), (C3'') became labelled child steps inside the case or claim steps that introduce them.
These prose nodes end at \end{equation} because the author never punctuates after displays; the finishing step's ends-mid-sentence warning is a false alarm.

Every paragraph starts with \vskip 1em, so the sentence-start check flags nearly all steps and prose nodes (warnings left); two steps starting with '(c)' or '$\omega$' were flagged as errors, so their statements keep the leading \vskip 1em.
The type-I Haag-duality claim includes the following 'In fact ...' sentence (the tensor splitting it asserts); the proof starts at 'A simple proof goes as follows:'.

metadata.extraction_comment: Remaining 'factor' defined-term warnings for DP1 are uses of 'factor' in the von Neumann algebra sense (M is a factor), not factor states, and were left without edges.

nodes.statement: A theorem of Takesaki's [Ta, also see AcC] says that conditional expectation E_c preserving a faithful normal state phi on mathcal M exists if and only if the modular group sigma=(sigma_t:t in R) associated with phi, which preserves mathcal M, also preserves mathcal N, i.e. sigma_t(x) in mathcal N for all t in R and x in mathcal N.
conclusions: A theorem of Takesaki's [Ta, also see AcC] says that conditional expectation E_c preserving a faithful normal state phi on mathcal M exists if and only if the modular group sigma=(sigma_t:t in R) associated with phi, which preserves mathcal M, also preserves mathcal N, i.e.

Let $v_1,v_2,...,v_d$ be a family of bounded operators on a Hilbert space
${\mathcal K}$ so that $\sum_{1 \le k \le d} v_kv_k^*=I$. Then there exists a unique up to
isomorphism Hilbert space ${\mathcal H}$, a projection $P$ on ${\mathcal K}$ and a family of isometries
$\{S_k:,\;1 \le k \le d \}$ satisfying Cuntz's relation so that
\begin{equation}
PS^{*}_{k}P=S_k^*P=v^*_k
\end{equation}
for all $1 \le k \le d$ and ${\mathcal K}$ is cyclic for the representation i.e. the vectors
$\{ S_I{\mathcal K}: |I| < \infty \}$ are total in ${\mathcal H}$.

Moreover the following holds:

\noindent (a) $\Lambda^n(P) \uparrow I$ as $n \uparrow \infty$ where $\Lambda(X)=\sum_k S_kXS_k^*$;

\noindent (b) For any $D \in {\mathcal B}_{\tau}({\mathcal K})=\{x \in {\mathcal B}({\mathcal K}): \tau(x)=\sum_{1 \le k \le d} v_kxv_k^*=x \}$, 
$\Lambda^n(D) \rightarrow X'$ weakly as $n \rightarrow \infty$ for some $X'$ in the commutant $\{S_k,S^*_k: 1 \le k \le d \}'$ so that $PX'P=D$. Moreover
the self adjoint elements in the commutant $\{S_k,S^*_k: 1 \le k \le d \}'$ is isometrically
order isomorphic with the self adjoint elements in ${\mathcal B}_{\tau}({\mathcal K})$ via the
surjective map $X' \rightarrow PX'P$, where ${\mathcal B}_{\tau}({\mathcal K})=\{x \in {\mathcal B}({\mathcal K}): \sum_{1 \le k \le d }
v_kxv^*_k=x \}.$

\noindent (c) $\{v_k,v^*_k,\;1 \le k \le d \}' \subseteq {\mathcal B}_{\tau}({\mathcal K})$ and equality holds if and only if
$P \in \{S_k,S_k,\;1 \le k \le d \}''$.

\vskip 1em 
If $(w_i)$ be another such an Popescu elements on a Hilbert space ${\mathcal K}'$ such that there exists an operator 
$u:{\mathcal K} \rightarrow {\mathcal K}'$ so that $\sum_k w_kuv_k^*=u$ then there exists an operator $U:{\mathcal H}_v \rightarrow {\mathcal H}_w$ so 
that $\pi'(x)U=U\pi(x)$ where $({\mathcal H}_w,\pi',S'_i)$ are Popescu dilation of $(w_i)$ and $\pi'$ is the associated
minimal representation of ${\mathcal O}_d$. In particular $U$ is isometry, unitary if $u$ is so respectively. If $u$ is unitary 
and ${\mathcal K}={\mathcal K}'$ then we can as well take ${\mathcal H}_v={\mathcal H}_w$.

Following Popescu [Po] we define a completely positive map
$R: {\mathcal O}_d \rightarrow {\mathcal B}({\mathcal K})$ by
\begin{equation}
R(s_Is^*_J)=v_Iv^*_J
\end{equation}
for all $|I|,|J| < \infty$. The representation $S_1,..,S_d$ of ${\mathcal O}_d$ on ${\mathcal H}$ thus may be taken to be the Stinespring
dilation of $R$ [BR, vol-2] and uniqueness up to unitary equivalence follows from uniqueness of the Stinespring
representation. That ${\mathcal K}$ is cyclic for the representation follows from the minimality property of the Stinespring
dilation. 

\vskip 1em 
For (a) let $Q$ be the limiting projection of $\Lambda^n(P)$ as $n \uparrow \infty$. Then we have $\Lambda(Q)=Q$ i.e. $Q\Lambda(I-Q)Q=0$ 
and so $(I-Q)S_k^*Q=0$. Interchanging the role of $Q$ with $I-Q$, we get $QS_k^*(I-Q)=0$. This shows $QS_k^*=S_k^*Q$ for all $1 le k \le d$. 
Since $Q$ is a projection, taking adjoint in the relation, we get $Q \in \{S_k,S^*_k\}'$. That $Q \ge P$ is obvious since $\Lambda^n(P) \ge P$ 
for all $n \ge 1$. In particular $QS_If=S_If$ for all $f \in {\mathcal K}$ and $|I| < \infty$. Hence $Q=I$ by the
cyclicity of ${\mathcal K}$. 

\vskip 1em 
For (b) essentially we deffer from the argument used in Theorem 5.1 in [BJKW]. We fix any $D
\in {\mathcal B}_{\tau}({\mathcal K})$ and note that $P\Lambda_k(D)P=\tau_k(D)=D$ for any $k \ge 1$. Thus for any integers $n > m$
we have
$$\Lambda_m(P)\Lambda_n(D)\Lambda_m(P)=\Lambda_m(P\Lambda_{n-m}(D)P)=\Lambda_m(D)$$
Hence for any fixed $m \ge 1$ limit $<f,\Lambda_n(D)g>$ as $n \rightarrow \infty$ exists for all
$f,g \in \Lambda_m(P)$. Since the family of operators $\Lambda_n(D)$ is uniformly bounded and $\Lambda_m(P) \uparrow I$
as $m \rightarrow \infty$, a standard density argument guarantees that the weak operator limit of $\Lambda_n(D)$ exists as
$n \rightarrow \infty$. Let $X'$ be the limit. So $\Lambda(X')=X'$, by Cuntz's relation, $X' \in \{S_k,S^*_k:1 \le k \le k \}'$.
Since $P\Lambda_n(D)P=D$ for all $n \ge 1$, we also conclude that $PX'P=D$ by taking limit $n \rightarrow \infty$. Conversely,
it is obvious that $P\{ S_k,S^*_k:\; k \ge 1 \}'P \subseteq {\mathcal B}_{\tau}({\mathcal K})$. Hence
we can identify $P\{S_k,S^*_k:\; k \ge 1 \}'P$ with ${\mathcal B}_{\tau}({\mathcal K})$.

\vskip 1em
Further it is obvious that $X'$ is self-adjoint if and only if $D=PX'P$ is self-adjoint ( since $\Lambda^n(P) \uparrow I$ as $n \uparrow \infty$, 
by taking limit $\Lambda^n(PXP)=\Lambda^n(PX^*P)$ shows that $X^*=X$ if $D^*=D$ ). Now fix any self-adjoint element $D \in {\mathcal B}_{\tau}({\mathcal K})$. Since 
the identity operator on ${\mathcal K}$ is an element in ${\mathcal B}_{\tau}({\mathcal K})$ for any $\alpha \ge 0$ for which $- \alpha P  \le D \le \alpha P$, we have $\alpha 
\Lambda_n(P) \le \Lambda_n(D) \le \alpha \Lambda_n(P)$ for all $n \ge 1$. By taking limit $n \rightarrow \infty$ we
conclude that $- \alpha I \le X' \le \alpha I$, where $PX'P=D$. Since operator norm of a self-adjoint element $A$
in a Hilbert space is given by
$$||A||= \mbox{inf}_{\alpha \ge 0}\{\alpha: - \alpha I  \le A \le \alpha I \}$$
we conclude that $||X'|| \le ||D||$. That $||D||=||PX'P|| \le ||X'||$ is obvious, $P$ being a
projection. Thus the map is isometrically order isomorphic taking self-adjoint elements of the commutant
to self-adjoint elements of ${\mathcal B}_{\tau}({\mathcal K})$.

\vskip 1em
We are left to prove (c). Inclusion is trivial. For the last part, we assume first that $P \in \pi({\mathcal O}_d)''$. For any element $D$
in ${\mathcal B}_{\tau}({\mathcal K})$ there exists an element $X'$ in $\{S_k,S^*_k,\;1 \le k \le d\}'$ so that $PX'P=D$. Since $P$ commutes with $X'$, 
we verify that 
$$Dv^*_k= PX'PS^*_kP=PX'S^*_kP=PS^*_kX'P=PS^*_kPX'P=v^*_kD$$ 
We also have $D^* \in {\mathcal B}_{\tau}({\mathcal K})$ and thus $D^*v^*_k=v^*_kD^*$. Hence $D \in \{v_k,v^*_k: 1 \le k \le d \}'$. Since $P\pi_{\hat{\omega}}
({\mathcal O}_d)'P = {\mathcal B}({\mathcal K})_{\tau}$, we conclude that ${\mathcal B}({\mathcal K})_{\tau} \subseteq {\mathcal M}'$. Thus equality holds whenever
$P \in \{S_k,S_k^*,\;1 \le k \le d \}''$. 

\vskip 1em 
For the converse note that by commutant lifting property self-adjoint elements
of the commutant $\{S_k,S^*_k,1 \le k \le d \}'$ is order isometric with the algebra ${\mathcal M}'$ via the map $X' \rightarrow PX'P$.
Hence $P \in \{S_k,S^*_k,1 \le k \le d \}''$ by Proposition 4.2 in [BJKW]. 

\vskip 1em 
For the proof of intertwining relation and their property we refer to main body of the proof of 
Theorem 5.1 in [BJKW].

\noindent (b) Function $C: {\mathcal I} \times {\mathcal I} \rightarrow \mathbb{C}$ with the following properties:

\noindent (i) $C(\emptyset, \emptyset)=1$;

\noindent (ii) for any function $\lambda:{\mathcal I} \rightarrow \mathbb{C}$ with finite support we have

$$\psi_{\Omega}(X) = <\Omega, X \Omega>$$
Let $P$ be the projection on the closed subspace ${\mathcal K}$ generated by the vectors $\{S^*_I\Omega: |I| < \infty \}$ and 
\begin{equation}
v_k=PS_kP
\end{equation}
for $1 \le k \le d$. Then following holds:

\vskip 1em
\noindent (a) $\{v^*_I\Omega: |I| < \infty \}$ is total in ${\mathcal K}$.

\noindent (b) $\sum_{1 \le k \le d} v_kv_k^*=I$;

\noindent (c) $S_k^*P=PS_k^*P$ for all $1 \le k \le d$; 

\noindent (d) For any $I=(i_1,i_2,...,i_k),J=(j_1,j_2,...,j_l)$ with $|I|,|J| < \infty$ we have 
\begin{equation} 
\psi(s_Is^*_J)= <\Omega,v_Iv^*_J\Omega>
\end{equation} 
and the vectors $\{ S_If: f \in {\mathcal K},\;|I| < \infty \}$ are total in
the GNS Hilbert space associated with $({\mathcal O}_d,\psi)$. Further such a family $({\mathcal K},\;v_k,\;1 \le k \le d,\;\omega)$ satisfying
(a) to (d) is determined uniquely up to isomorphism. 

\vskip 1em
Conversely given a Popescu system $({\mathcal K},v_k,\;1 \le k \le d,\Omega)$ satisfying (a) and (b) there exists a unique   state 
$\psi$ on ${\mathcal O}_d$ so that (c) and (d) are satisfied.

Furthermore the following statements are valid:
\vskip 1em
\noindent (e)  If the normal state $\phi(x)=<\Omega,x \Omega>$ on the von-Neumann algebra
${\mathcal M}=\{ v_i, v^*_i \}''$ is invariant for the Markov map $\tau(x)=\sum_{1 \le k

on ${\mathcal M}$.

\noindent (i) $\psi$ is an ergodic state for $({\mathcal O}_d,\lambda)$; 

\noindent (ii) $({\mathcal M},\tau,\phi)$ is ergodic;

\noindent (ii) ${\mathcal M}$ is a factor.

Let $({\mathcal H},\pi,\Omega)$ be the GNS representation of a $\lambda$ invariant state 
$\psi$ on ${\mathcal O}_d$ and $P$ be the support projection of the normal state $\psi_{\Omega}(X)=<\Omega,X\Omega>$ in the 
von-Neumann algebra $\pi({\mathcal O}_d)''$. Then the following holds:

\vskip 1em
\noindent (a) $P$ is a sub-harmonic projection for the endomorphism $\Lambda(X)=\sum_k S_kXS^*_k$ on $\pi({\mathcal O}_d)''$
i.e. $\Lambda(P) \ge P$ satisfying the following:

\vskip 1em 
\noindent (i) $\Lambda_n(P) \uparrow I$ as $n \uparrow \infty$;

\vskip 1em 
\noindent (ii) $PS^*_kP=S^*_kP,\;\;1 \le k \le d$;

\vskip 1em 
\noindent (iii) $\sum_{1 \le k \le d} v_kv_k^*=I$ 

where $S_k=\pi(s_k)$ and $v_k=PS_kP$ for $1 \le k \le d$;

\vskip 1em
\noindent (b) For any $I=(i_1,i_2,...,i_k),J=(j_1,j_2,...,j_l)$ with $|I|,|J| < \infty$ we have $\psi(s_Is^*_J) =
<\Omega,v_Iv^*_J\Omega>$ and the vectors $\{ S_If: f \in {\mathcal K},\;|I| < \infty \}$ are total in ${\mathcal H}$;

\vskip 1em
\noindent (c) The von-Neumann algebra ${\mathcal M}=P\pi({\mathcal O}_d)''P$, acting on the Hilbert space
${\mathcal K}$ i.e. the range of $P$, is generated by $\{v_k,v^*_k:1 \le k \le d \}''$ and the normal state
$\phi(x)=<\Omega,x \Omega>$ is faithful on the von-Neumann algebra ${\mathcal M}$.

\vskip 1em 
\noindent (d) The self-adjoint part of the commutant of $\pi({\mathcal O}_d)'$ is norm and order isomorphic to the space
of self-adjoint fixed points of the completely positive map $\tau$. The isomorphism takes $X' \in \pi({\mathcal O}_d)'$
onto $PX'P \in {\mathcal B}_{\tau}({\mathcal K})$, where ${\mathcal B}_{\tau}({\mathcal K}) = \{ x \in {\mathcal B}({\mathcal K}): \tau(x)=x \}$ and 
$\tau(x)=\sum_kv_kxv^*_k,\;x \in {\mathcal B}({\mathcal K})$. Furthermore ${\mathcal M}' = {\mathcal B}_{\tau}({\mathcal K})$.

\vskip 1em
Conversely let ${\mathcal M}$ be a von-Neumann algebra generated by a family $\{v_k: 1 \le k \le d \}$ of bounded operators
on a Hilbert space ${\mathcal K}$ so that $\sum_kv_kv_k^*=1$ and the commutant 
\begin{equation} 
{\mathcal M}'=\{x \in {\mathcal B}({\mathcal K}): \sum_k v_kxv_k^*=x \}
\end{equation} 
Then the Popescu dilation $({\mathcal H},P,S_k,\;1 \le k \le d)$ described in Theorem 2.1 satisfies the following:

\vskip 1em 
\noindent (i) $P \in \{S_k,S^*_k,\;1 \le k \le d \}''$;

\vskip 1em 
\noindent (ii) For any faithful normal $\tau-$invariant state $\phi$ on ${\mathcal M}$ there exists a state $\psi$ on ${\mathcal O}_d$ defined by
$$\psi(s_Is^*_J)=\phi(v_Iv^*_J),\;|I|,|J| < \infty $$
such that the GNS space associated with $({\mathcal M},\phi)$ is the support projection
for $\psi$ in $\pi({\mathcal O}_d)''$ satisfying (a)-(d). 

\vskip 1em
Further for a given $\lambda$-invariant state $\psi$, the family $({\mathcal K},{\mathcal M},v_k\;1 \le k \le d,\phi)$ satisfying (a)-(d) 
is determined uniquely up to unitary conjugation. 

\vskip 1em
\noindent (e) $\phi$ is a faithful normal $\tau$-invariant state on ${\mathcal M}$. Furthermore the following statements are equivalent:

\noindent (i) $({\mathcal O}_d,\lambda,\psi)$ is ergodic;

\noindent (ii) $({\mathcal M},\tau,\phi)$ is ergodic;

\noindent (iii) ${\mathcal M}$ is a factor.

generated by $S_IS^*_J\Omega$, $Y$ is a scalar. $Y$ being a non-zero projection, it is

note that for any invariant element $D$ in ${\mathcal B}({\mathcal K})$ there exists an element $X'$ in $\pi({\mathcal O}_d)'$ so that $PX'P=D$.
Since $P \in \pi({\mathcal O}_d)''$ we note that $(1-P)X'P=0$.

and so its support projection.

By Theorem 3.6 in [Mo1] the Markov semi-group $({\mathcal M},\tau,\phi)$ is ergodic if and
only if $(\pi({\mathcal O}_d)'',\Lambda,\psi_{\Omega})$ is ergodic ( here we need to recall by (a) that
$\Lambda_n(P) \uparrow I$ as $n \uparrow \infty$ ). By a standard result [Ev, also BJKW] $({\mathcal M},\tau,\phi)$

This shows equivalence of (ii) and (iii) follows by a standard result [La,Fr] in non-commutative ergodic theory. This completes the proof.

Let $\psi$ be a $\lambda$ invariant factor state on ${\mathcal O}_d$ and $({\mathcal H},\pi,\Omega)$
be its GNS representation. Then the following holds:

\noindent (a) The closed subgroup $H=\{z \in S^1: \psi \beta_z =\psi \}$ is equal to 

$$\{z \in S^1: \beta_z \mbox{extends to an automorphism of } \pi({\mathcal O}_d)'' \} $$ 

\noindent (b) Let ${\mathcal O}_d^{H}$ be the fixed point sub-algebra in ${\mathcal O}_d$ under the action of gauge group $\{ \beta_z: z \in H \}$. Then  
$\pi({\mathcal O}_d^{H})'' = \pi(\mbox{UHF}_d)''$.

\noindent (c) If $H$ is a finite cyclic group of $k$ many elements and $\pi(\mbox{UHF}_d)''$ is a factor, 
then $\pi({\mathcal O}_d)'' \bigcap \pi(\mbox{UHF}_d)' \equiv \mathbb{C}^m$ where $1 \le m \le k$.

uniquely to an automorphism of $\pi({\mathcal O}_d)''_{{|}_{{\mathcal H}}}$ commuting with the restriction of the canonical endomorphism

Let $\omega,\psi$ be as in Proposition 3.2 with Popescu system $({\mathcal K},{\mathcal M},$ $v_k,\Omega)$ be 
taken as in Proposition 2.4 i.e. on support projection. Then the centre of 
$\pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d)''$ is completely atomic and the element 
$E_0=[\pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d)' \vee \pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes 
\mbox{UHF}_d)''\Omega]$ is a minimal projection in the centre of $\pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d)''$ and the centre is invariant for both $\Lambda$ and $\tilde{\Lambda}$. Furthermore the 
following holds:

\vskip 1em 
\noindent (a) The centre of $\pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d)''$ has the following two disjoint
possibilities:

\vskip 1em 
\noindent (i) There exists a positive integer $m \ge 1$ such that the centre is generated by the family of minimal
orthogonal projections $\{ \Lambda_k(E_0): 0 \le k \le m-1 \}$ where $m \ge 1$ is the least positive integer so that
$\Lambda^m(E_0)=E_0$. In such a case $\{z: z^m = 1 \} \subseteq H$;

\vskip 1em 
\noindent (ii) The family of minimal nonzero orthogonal projections $\{ E_k: k \in \mathbb{Z} \}$ where $E_k= \Lambda^k(E_0)$
for $k \ge 0$ and $E_k= S^*_IE_0S_I$ for $k < 0$ where $|I|=-k$ and independent of multi-index $I$ generates
the centre and $H=S^1$; 

\vskip 1em
\noindent (b) $\Lambda(E)=\tilde{\Lambda}(E) $ for any $E$ in the centre of $\pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d)''$

\vskip 1em 
\noindent (c) If $\Lambda(E_0)=E_0$ then $E_0=1$.

\noindent (b) ${\mathcal I}={\mathcal I}_0$ if and only if $\omega$ is pure. 

Further the following statements are equivalent: 

\noindent (c) ${\mathcal I} = \pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d)''$; 

\noindent (d) $\pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes {\mathcal O}_d)''= {\mathcal B}(\tilde{{\mathcal H}} \otimes_{{\mathcal K}} {\mathcal H})$;

\noindent (e) $\pi(\tilde{{\mathcal O}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d )''= {\mathcal B}(\tilde{{\mathcal H}} \otimes_{{\mathcal K}} {\mathcal H})$;

\vskip 1em
In such a case (i.e. if any of (c),(d) and (e) is true ) the following statements are also true: 

\noindent (f) $\pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d)''$ is a type-I von-Neumann algebra with centre equal 
to $\{ U_z: z \in H \}''$ where $U_z$ is defined in Proposition 3.2. 

\noindent (g) $\omega$ is a pure state on ${\mathcal B}$.

algebra with centre equal to $\{U_z: z \in H_0 \}''$ where $H_0$ is a subgroup of $H$.

Along the same line of the proof of Proposition 2.5 (b) we get $\{\beta_z: z \in H \}$ invariant elements 
in $\pi({\mathcal O}_d \otimes \tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d)''$ is $\pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d)''$ where factor property 
of $\pi({\mathcal O}_d)''$ is crucial as in proof of Proposition 2.5 (b). Same holds for $\pi(\mbox{UHF}_d \otimes \tilde{{\mathcal O}}_d)''$ as 
$\pi(\tilde{{\mathcal O}}_d)''$ is a factor. Here we comment that factor property of $\pi(\tilde{{\mathcal O}}_d)''$ can be
ensured whenever $\psi$ is an extremal element in $K_{\omega'}$ (See Proposition 3.2 (a) ). 

\vskip 1em
For (b) we will first prove ${\mathcal I}_0={\mathcal I}$ if $\omega$ is pure. As by definition ${\mathcal I}_0 \subseteq {\mathcal I}$, it is enough if we show 
${\mathcal I}'_0 \subseteq {\mathcal I}'$. Let $X \in {\mathcal I}'_0$ i.e. $X$ commutes with $\{ U_z:z \in H\}''$ and $\pi(\mbox{UHF}_d \otimes 
\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d)''$. For each $k \in \hat{H}$, $F_kXF_k$ is an element in the commutant of $F_k\pi(\mbox{UHF}_d \otimes 
\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d)''F_k$. $\omega$ being pure each representation $\pi$ restricted to $F_k$ is irreducible and thus
$F_kXF_k = c_k F_k$ for some scalars $c_k$. Hence $X=\sum_k c_k F_k \in {\mathcal I}'=\{U_z: z \in H \}''$. 

\vskip 1em
For the converse we need to show that the restriction of $\pi(\mbox{UHF}_d \otimes 
\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d)''$ to $F'_0$ is pure. Let $X$ be an element on the subspace $F'_0$ and in the commutant 
of $F'_0\pi(\mbox{UHF}_d \otimes \tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d)''F'_0$, ( which in our earlier notation $E'$ in Proposition 3.3 ). 
Then $X$ commutes with each $F_k$ for $k \in \hat{H}$ and $\pi(\mbox{UHF}_d \otimes 
\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d)''F_k$ as $F'_0 \le F_0$ and $F_k$ are orthogonal to 
$F'_0$ for $k \neq 0$. So $X$ commutes with $\{U_z: z \in H \}''$ and 
$\pi(\mbox{UHF}_d \otimes \tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d)''$ i.e. $X \in {\mathcal I}'_0$. By our assumption ${\mathcal I}_0={\mathcal I}$, we have now
$X \in {\mathcal I}'$ which is equal to $\{F_k: k \in \hat{H} \}''$ and so $X=cF_0$ 
for some scalar $c_0$. This shows that $F'_0=F_0$ and $\omega$ is pure.    

\vskip 1em
(c) implies (d): $\{U_z: z \in H \}$ is a commuting family of unitaries such that $\beta_z(X)=U_zXU_z^*$ and 
thus by (c) $\{U_z: z \in H \}'' \subseteq \pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d)''$. Let $X$ be an 
element in the commutant of $\pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes {\mathcal O}_d)''$. Then 
$X$ commutes also with $\{U_z: z \in H \}''$ and thus $X \in \pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d)''$ by (c).
Hence $X$ is an element in the centre of $\pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d)''$ and so 
$X=\sum_k c_kE_k$ where $E_k$ are the minimal projections in the centre of $\pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d)''$ 
given in Proposition 3.3. However $X$ also 
commutes with $\pi({\mathcal O}_d)''$ by our assumption (c) and $\Lambda(E_k)=E_{k+1}$ for $k \in \hat{H}$.  
So $c_k=c_{k+1}$ and $X$ is a scalar multiple of unit operator. Hence (d) follows from (c). Along the same line we prove 
(c) implies (e). For a proof for (d) implies (c) and (e) implies (c), we simply apply (a).   

\vskip 1em
Now we will prove (f) and (g). That $\pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d)''$ is 
a type-I von-Neumann algebra ( with completely atomic centre ) follows by a theorem of [So] once we use (c). In the proof 
of Proposition 3.3 we have proved that the centre of $\pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d)''$ is 
$\{U_z: z \in H_0 \}''$ where $H_0 \subseteq H$. For equality in the present situation we simply use (c), as $\beta_w(U_z)=U_z$
for all $w,z \in H$, to conclude that $U_z$ is in the centre of $\pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d)''$. 

\vskip 1em
If (c) holds then ${\mathcal I}_0={\mathcal I}$ and thus (g) follows by (b). Here we will give another proof using the same idea to prove (f). 
Let $X$ be an element in the commutant of $\pi_0(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d)''$, where $\pi_0$ is the factor 
representation on the minimal central projection $E_0$ defined in Proposition 3.3. Then $X$ commutes with 
$\{U_z: z \in H \}''$ and so by (c) $X$ in an element in $\pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d)''$. 
So $X$ is in the centre of $\pi_0(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d)''$. $\pi_0$ being a factor representation
$X$ is a scalar multiple of $E_0$. Thus $\pi_0$ is an irreducible representation and so $\omega$ is pure. 

\vskip 1em
By Proposition 3.1 we recall that $\pi'_0$ is unitary equivalent to the GNS representation of $({\mathcal B},\omega)$. 
Thus $\pi'_0$ is irreducible if and only if $\omega$ is pure. So for a pure state $\omega$, 
for each $k \in \hat{H}_0$, $\pi_k$ being quasi-equivalent to $\pi'_k$, $\pi_k$ is a type-I factor 
representation of $\pi(\mbox{UHF}_d \otimes \tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d)''$. This completes the proof.

Now moving to $\{\beta_z: z \in H \}$ invariant elements in the duality relation above, we verify that 
adjoint Markov map of $(\tilde{{\mathcal M}}_0,\tilde{\tau},\phi)$ is given by 
$(\tilde{{\mathcal M}}'_0,\tau,\phi)$ where $\tilde{{\mathcal M}}'_0$, the commutant of $\tilde{{\mathcal M}}_0$ 
is taken in ${\mathcal B}({\mathcal K}_0)$ and ${\mathcal K}_0$ is the Hilbert subspace $P_0$ with $\Omega$ as
cyclic and separating vector for $\tilde{{\mathcal M}}_0$ in ${\mathcal K}_0$. Thus by Theorem 2.4 in [Mo3], 
there exists a sequence of elements $y_n \in \tilde{{\mathcal M}}'_0$ such that for each $m \ge 1$, 
$y_{m+n}\tau_n(y) \rightarrow \phi(y)1$ as $n \rightarrow \infty$ for all $y \in \tilde{{\mathcal M}}'_0 \subseteq {\mathcal B}({\mathcal K}_0)$. 
Thus $\omega$ is pure by Proposition 3.5 (e) once we recall ${\mathcal M}'=\tilde{{\mathcal M}}$ as $P=Q$ 
( and so ${\mathcal M}'_0 = \tilde{{\mathcal M}}_0$ ) by Proposition 3.5 (d). This completes the proof of
 purity property of $\omega$. 


\vskip 1em  
In the following we now prove the hardest part of the theorem namely $\tilde{{\mathcal F}}={\mathcal E}$ and ${\mathcal F}=\tilde{{\mathcal E}}$ if $\omega$ is pure. Proof uses extensively 
the general theory of quasi-equivalent representation of a $C^*$ algebra and we refer [BR1, Chapter 2.4.4] as a general reference.   

\vskip 1em 
We set unitary operator $V=\sum_k S_k\tilde{S}^*_k$. That $V$ is a unitary operator follows by Cuntz's relations and commuting property 
of $(S_i)$ and $(\tilde{S}_i)$. Further a simple computation shows that $V\pi(x)V^*=\pi(\theta(x))$ for all $x \in {\mathcal B} = {\mathcal B}_L \otimes {\mathcal B}_R$, 
identified with $\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d$ and $\theta$ is the right shift. We also have    
\begin{equation} 
\theta({\mathcal E})=V {\mathcal E} V^*= \sum_{k,k'}S_k\tilde{S}^*_k {\mathcal E} S^*_{k'}\tilde{S}_{k'}=\Lambda({\mathcal E}) \ge {\mathcal E}
\end{equation} 
Similarly we also have
\begin{equation} 
\theta(\tilde{{\mathcal F}}) \ge \tilde{{\mathcal F}} 
\end{equation}
So in particular we have $V(I-{\mathcal E})V^* \le I-{\mathcal E}$, i.e. $(I-{\mathcal E})V^*{\mathcal E}=0$.  
Also for any $X \in \pi({\mathcal O}_d)'$ we have $V^*\tilde{{\mathcal F}}X\Omega = 
\tilde{{\mathcal F}} \sum_k \tilde{S}_k X \tilde{S}_k^*\Omega$ as $S_k^*\Omega 
=\tilde{S}_k^*\Omega$. Thus $(I-\tilde{{\mathcal F}})V^*\tilde{{\mathcal F}}=0$ i.e. 
$V\tilde{{\mathcal F}}V^*=\Lambda(\tilde{{\mathcal F}}) \ge \tilde{{\mathcal F}}$. Similarly we also 
have 
\begin{equation} 
\theta^{-1}(\tilde{{\mathcal E}})=V^*\tilde{{\mathcal E}}V \ge \tilde{{\mathcal E}}\;\mbox{and}\; V^* {\mathcal F} V \ge {\mathcal F}
\end{equation} 
We also set two family of increasing projections for all natural numbers $n \in \mathbb{Z}$ as follows 
\begin{equation} 
{\mathcal E}_n=V^n {\mathcal E} (V^n)^*,\;\;\tilde{{\mathcal F}}_n=V^n\tilde{{\mathcal F}}(V^n)^*
\end{equation}

\vskip 1em 
Since $\beta_z(V)=V$ for all $z \in H$, $V \in \pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d)''$ by Proposition 3.4 as $\omega$ is pure. $\omega$ being also a factor state, we have $<f,V^ng> \rightarrow <f,\Omega><\Omega,g>$ as $n \rightarrow + \mbox{or} - \infty$ for any $f,g \in \pi({\mathcal B}_{loc})\Omega$ by Power's criteria [Pow] given in (1). Since such vectors are dense in the Hilbert space topology and the family $\{V^n:n \ge 1\}$ is uniformly bounded, we get $V^n \rightarrow |\Omega><\Omega|$ in weak operator topology as $n \rightarrow + \mbox{or} - \infty$.   

\vskip 1em 
For the time being we assume that $H$ is trivial. Otherwise the argument that follows here we can use for the representation $\pi_0$ of $\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d$ i.e. $\pi$ restricted to $[\pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d)\Omega]$. 

\vskip 1em 
We have following distinct cases: 

\vskip 1em 
\noindent {\bf Case 1.} ${\mathcal E} \neq I \;( \tilde{{\mathcal E}} \neq I)$. Let ${\mathcal E}_n \rightarrow {\mathcal E}_{-\infty}$ as $n \rightarrow -\infty$ and thus $V{\mathcal E}_{-\infty}V^*={\mathcal E}_{-\infty}$. We claim that either ${\mathcal E}_{-\infty} = |\Omega><\Omega|$ or ${\mathcal E}_{-\infty}$ is a proper infinite dimensional projection i.e. if ${\mathcal E}_{- \infty}$ is a finite projection then ${\mathcal E}_{- \infty}=|\Omega><\Omega|$. Suppose not then the finite subspace is shift invariant. In particular there exists a unit  vector $f$ orthogonal to $\Omega$ such that $Vf=zf$ for some $z \in S^1$ and this contradicts weak mixing property i.e. $V^n \rightarrow |\Omega><\Omega|$ in weak operator topology proved above as point spectrum of $V$ has only $1$ with spectral multiplicity $1$. 

\vskip 1em 
If ${\mathcal E}_{-\infty}$ is infinite dimensional we can get a unitary operator $U_0$ from 
$F_0=\tilde{{\mathcal H}} \otimes_{{\mathcal K}} {\mathcal H}$ onto ${\mathcal E}_{- \infty}$ and 
via the unitary map we can get a sequence of increasing projections $U_0{\mathcal E}_nU^*_0$ in ${\mathcal E}_{- \infty}$ and note that $U_0{\mathcal E}_nU_0^*=V^nU_0 {\mathcal E} U_0^*(V^n)^*$. Note that if ${\mathcal E}_{- \infty}$ is infinite dimension the process will not stop in finite step. Thus we have $F_0 \ominus \Omega = \oplus_{1 \le k \le n_{{\mathcal E}}} F(k)$ where the index set is either singleton or infinity and each $F(k)$ will give a system of imprimitivity with respect to $V$, where $F(1)
=F_0-{\mathcal E}_{-\infty}$. Further $\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d$ being a simple $C^*$-algebra, each such imprimitivity system 
is of Mackey index $\aleph_0$ [Mo3,section 4]: We fix a nonzero $f \in {\mathcal E}-\theta^{-1}({\mathcal E}) \neq 0$ otherwise ${\mathcal E}=I$ as $\theta^n({\mathcal E}) \uparrow I$ as $n \rightarrow \infty$. $\pi_f:x \rightarrow \theta^{-1}(x)f$ gives a representation of $\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d={\mathcal B}_L$ and we check that $[\pi_f(\theta^{-1}({\mathcal B}_L)''f] \le {\mathcal E}-\theta^{-1}({\mathcal E})$ 
as $f \perp [\theta^{-1}(\pi({\mathcal B}_R)')\Omega] \ge [\theta^{-1}(\pi({\mathcal B}_L))\Omega]$. Thus simplicity 
ensures that ${\mathcal E} - \theta^{-1}({\mathcal E})$ is a projection of dimension $\aleph_0$. Further $n_{\mathcal E}$ is either $1$
or $\aleph_0$ since $F_0$ is separable.   

\vskip 1em 
Since $\tilde{{\mathcal F}}$ is also a proper projection, same argument is valid for $\tilde{{\mathcal F}}$ with $\tilde{{\mathcal F}}_{-\infty}=
\mbox{lim}_{n \rightarrow -\infty} \theta^n(\tilde{{\mathcal F}})$ i.e. we can write $F_0 \ominus \Omega = \oplus_{1 \le k \le n_{\tilde{{\mathcal F}}}} \tilde{H}(k)$, where each $\tilde{H}(k)$ give rises to a system of imprimitivity with respect to $V$ where each system of imprimitivity is of Mackey index $\aleph_0$ where $\tilde{F}(1) = F_0-\tilde{{\mathcal F}}_{-\infty}$ 
and $n_{\tilde{{\mathcal F}}}$ is either $1$ or $\aleph_0$.        

\vskip 1em 
In the following we use temporary notation $H$ for Hilbert subspace $F_0$. For a cardinal number $n$, we 
amplify a representation $\pi:{\mathcal B} \rightarrow {\mathcal B}(H)$ of the $C^*$ algebra ${\mathcal B}$ to $n$ fold direct sum 
$n\pi=\oplus_{1 \le k \le n } \pi_k $ acting on $nH=\oplus_{1 \le k \le n } H_k$  defining by 
$$n\pi(x) (\oplus \zeta_k) = \oplus (\pi(x)\zeta_k)$$ 
where $\pi_k = \pi$ is the representation of ${\mathcal B}=\mbox{UHF}_d \otimes \tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d$ 
on $H_k=H$ where $H =[\pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d)\Omega]$. We also 
extend $\bar{\tilde{F}} = \oplus \tilde{F}_{\alpha}$, $\bar{E} = \oplus E_{\alpha}$ and $\bar{V}=\oplus_{1 \le k \le n} V_k$ respectively. We also set notation $\Omega_k=\oplus_{1 \le k \le n}\delta^k_j\Omega$. 

\vskip 1em 
Thus by Mackey's theorem, there exists a cardinal number $n \in \aleph_0$ and a unitary operator $U: nH \rightarrow nH$ so that 
$\bar{V}=U\bar{V}U^*$ and $\bar{{\mathcal E}}=U\bar{\tilde{{\mathcal F}}}U^*$. We set a representation 
$\pi^U:{\mathcal B} \rightarrow {\mathcal B}(nH)$ by $\pi^U(x)= Un\pi(x)U^*$
and rewrite the above identity as 
$$\oplus_{1 \le k \le n}[\pi_k(\mbox{UHF}_d)'\Omega_k] = \oplus_{1 \le k \le n}
[\pi^U_k(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d)''\Omega_k]$$
where $\pi^U_k(x)=U\pi_k(x)U^*$. Note that by our construction we 
can ensure $U\Omega_k=\Omega_k$ for all $1 \le k \le n$ as the operator 
intertwining between two imprimitivity systems are acting on the orthogonal 
subspace of the projection generated by vectors $\{\Omega_k:1 \le k \le n\}$. 

\vskip 1em 
We claim ${\mathcal E}=\tilde{{\mathcal F}}$. Suppose not i.e. $\tilde{{\mathcal F}} < {\mathcal E}$. In such a case we 
have
$$\oplus_{1 \le k \le n}[\pi_k(\mbox{UHF}_d)'\Omega_k] < \oplus_{1 \le k \le n}
[\pi^u_k(\mbox{UHF}_d)'\Omega_k]$$
Alternatively 
$$\oplus_{1 \le k \le n}[\pi_k(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d)''\Omega_k] < \oplus_{1 \le k \le n}
[\pi^u_k(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d)''\Omega_k]$$

\vskip 1em 
Thus in principle we can repeat our construction now with $\pi^U$ and so we 
get a strict partial ordered set of quasi-equivalent representation of ${\mathcal B}$. 
In the following we now aim to employ formal set theory to bring a contradiction 
on our starting assumption that $\tilde{{\mathcal F}} < {\mathcal E}$. 

\vskip 1em 
To that end we need to deal with more then one representation of ${\mathcal B}$. For the rest of the proof we reset notation $\pi_0$ for $\pi$ used for the pure representation of 
${\mathcal B}$ in $H_0 =[\pi_0({\mathcal B})\Omega_0]$ where $\Omega_0$ is the cyclic vector, the reset notation for $\Omega$. Let ${\mathcal P}$ be the collection of representation $(\pi,H_{\pi},\Omega)$ 
quasi-equivalent to $\pi_0:{\mathcal B} \rightarrow {\mathcal B}(H_0)$ with a shift invariant vector state $\omega(x)=<\Omega,\pi(x)\Omega>$ i.e. $\omega(\pi(\theta(x))=\omega(\pi(x))$. So there exists 
minimal cardinal numbers $n_{\pi},n_0(\pi)$ so that $n_{\pi}H_{\pi}$ is unitary equivalent to $n_0(\pi)\pi_0$. Thus for such an element $(\pi,H_{\pi},\Omega_{\pi})$ we can associate 
two cardinal numbers $n_{\pi}$ and $n_0(\pi)$ and without loss of generality we assume that $H_{\pi} \subseteq n_0(\pi)H_0$ and $n_{\pi}H_{\pi}=n_0(\pi)H_0.$  $\pi_0$ being a pure 
representation, any element $\pi \in {\mathcal P}$ is a type-I factor representation of ${\mathcal B}$. The interesting point here that $\displaystyle{\oplus_{\pi \in {\mathcal P} }}\pi$ is also an element in ${\mathcal P}$ 
with associated cardinal numbers $\sum_{\pi} n_{\pi}$ and $\sum_{\pi} n_0(\pi)$. We say $(\pi_1,H_{\pi_1},\Omega^1) \prec (\pi_2,H_{\pi_2},\Omega^2)$ if there exists an 
isometry $U:n_{\pi_1} H_{\pi_1} \rightarrow n_{\pi_2} H_{\pi_2}$ so that 

\vskip 1em 
\noindent (C1) For each $1 \le \alpha \le n_{\pi_1} $ we have 
$U \Omega^1_{\alpha} = \Omega^2_{\alpha'}$ for some 
$1 \le \alpha' \le n_{\pi_2}$;        

\noindent (C2) $n_{\pi_2}\pi_2(x)E'_2 = U n_{\pi_1}\pi_1(x) U^* $ where ${\mathcal E}'_2 \in n_{\pi_2}\pi_2({\mathcal B})'$; 
 
\noindent (C3) $\oplus_{1 \le \alpha \le n_{\pi_1} }[\pi^{\alpha}_1(\mbox{UHF}_d)'\Omega^1_{\alpha}] < \oplus_{1 \le 
\alpha \le n_{\pi_2}}[\pi^{\alpha}_2(\mbox{UHF}_d)'\Omega^2_{\alpha}]E'_2$.

\vskip 1em 
In the inequality we explicitly used that both Hilbert spaces are subspaces of $nH_0$ for some possibly larger cardinal 
number $n$. That the partial order is non-reflexive follows as $(\pi,H,\Omega) \prec (\pi,H,\Omega)$ contradicts 
(C3) as $I=E_2'$. Partial order property follows easily. If $\pi_1 \prec \pi_2$ and $\pi_2 \prec \pi_3$ then $\pi_1 \prec \pi_3$. 
If $U_{12}$ and $U_{23}$ are isometric operators that satisfies (C1)-(C3) respectively, then $U_{13}=U_{23}U_{12}$ will 
do the job for $\pi_1$ and $\pi_3$. Thus $\pi^U \in {\mathcal P}$ and by our starting assumption that $\tilde{{\mathcal F}} \neq {\mathcal E}$ we also 
check that $\pi_0 \prec \pi^U$. Thus going via the isomorphism we also check that for a given element $\pi \in {\mathcal P}$ there exists 
an element $\pi' \in {\mathcal P}$ so that $\pi \prec \pi'$. Thus ${\mathcal P}_0$ is a non empty set and has at least one infinite chain containing $\pi_0$.
 
\vskip 1em 
However by Hausdorff maximality theorem there exists a non-empty maximal totally ordered subset ${\mathcal P}_0$ of ${\mathcal P}$ 
containing $\pi_0$. We claim that $\pi_{max} = \oplus_{\pi \in {\mathcal P}_0} \pi$ on $H_{\pi_{max}}=\oplus_{\pi \in {\mathcal P}_0} H_{\pi} $ is an upper bound in ${\mathcal P}_0$. That $\pi_{max} \in {\mathcal P}$ is obvious. Further given an element $(H_{\pi_1},\pi_1,\Omega_1) \in {\mathcal P}_0$ there exists an element $(H_{\pi_2},\pi_2,\Omega_2) \in {\mathcal P}_0$ so that $\pi_1 \prec \pi_2$ by our starting remark as $\pi_0 \prec \pi^U$. By extending isometry $U_{12}$ to an isometry from $H_{\pi_1} \rightarrow n_{\pi_{max}} H_{\pi_{max}}$ trivially we get the required isometry that satisfies (C1),(C2) and (C3) where cardinal numbers $n_{\pi_{max}} = \sum_{\pi \in {\mathcal P}_0} n_{\pi} \in \aleph$. Thus by maximal property of ${\mathcal P}_0$ we have $\pi_{max} \in {\mathcal P}_0$. This brings a contradiction as by our construction $(\pi_{max},H_{\pi_{max}},\Omega) \prec (\pi_{max},H_{\pi_{max}},\Omega)$ as $\pi_{max} \in {\mathcal P}_0$ but partial order is strict. This contradicts our starting hypothesis that $\tilde{{\mathcal F}} < {\mathcal E}$. This completes the proof that $\tilde{{\mathcal F}}={\mathcal E}$ when ${\mathcal E} \neq I$. By symmetry of the argument we also get ${\mathcal F}=\tilde{{\mathcal E}}$ when $\tilde{{\mathcal E}} < 1$.  

\vskip 1em 
\noindent {\bf Case 2:} ${\mathcal E}=I \;(\tilde{{\mathcal E}}=I)$. We need to show $\tilde{{\mathcal F}}=I\;({\mathcal F}=I)$ respectively. Suppose not and assume that both $\tilde{{\mathcal F}}$ is a proper non-zero projection. 

\vskip 1em 
We set projection $G$ on the closed linear span of elements in the subspaces $[\theta^{-n}({\mathcal F})\pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d)''\Omega]$ for all $n \ge 0$. We recall that $\theta(X)=VXV^*$ 
where $V=\sum_k S_k\tilde{S}_k^*$ and $\theta^{-1}(X)=\tilde{\Lambda}(X)$ 
for $X \in \pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d)''$. Thus we have 
$$V^*\theta^{-n}({\mathcal F})\pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d)''\Omega$$
$$=\theta^{-n-1}({\mathcal F})V^*\pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d)''V\Omega$$
$$=\theta^{-n-1}({\mathcal F}) \tilde{\Lambda}(\pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d)''\Omega.$$
Thus $(1-G)V^*G=0$ i.e. $\theta(G) \ge G$. It is also clear that $\tilde{{\mathcal F}} \le G$ 
as the defining sequence of subspaces of $G$ goes to precisely $\tilde{{\mathcal F}}$ as $n \rightarrow \infty$ ( recall 
that $\theta^{-n}({\mathcal F})=\tilde{\Lambda}_n({\mathcal F}) \uparrow I$ strongly as $n \uparrow \infty$ ). Once more we have 
$\theta^n(G) \ge \theta^n(\tilde{{\mathcal F}}) = \Lambda^n(\tilde{{\mathcal F}}) \uparrow I$ as $n \uparrow 
\infty$.  

\vskip 1em 
If $G$ is a proper projection we can follow the steps as in the case 1 to find a unitary operator 
$U:nH \rightarrow nH$ with $U\Omega_k=\Omega_k$ and $U\bar{V}U^*=\bar{V}$ so that $U\bar{G}U^*=\bar{\tilde{{\mathcal F}}}$. 
We consider the subset ${\mathcal P}_G$ of elements in ${\mathcal P}$ for which ${\mathcal E}_{\pi}=1$ and 
$\{\theta^{-n}({\mathcal F}_{\pi}):n \ge 0 \}$ commutes with $\tilde{{\mathcal F}}_{\pi}$ 
and modify the strict partial ordering by modifying (C3) as  

\vskip 1em 
\noindent (C3') $\oplus_{1 \le \alpha \le n_{\pi_1} }[\pi^{\alpha}_1(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d)''\Omega^1_{\alpha}] <  \oplus_{1 \le 
\alpha \le n_{\pi_2}}[\pi^{\alpha}_2(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d)''\Omega^2_{\alpha}]E'_2$

\noindent So we also get $\pi^U \in {\mathcal P}_G$ and $\pi_0 \prec \pi^U$ and going along the same line we conclude that 
$G=\tilde{{\mathcal F}}$. Thus we conclude that $G$ is either equal to $1$ or $G=\tilde{{\mathcal F}}$. 

\vskip 1em 
\noindent {\bf Sub-case 1 of case 2:} If $G=I$ then ${\mathcal F} G = {\mathcal F}$ and so $[{\mathcal F}\pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d)''\Omega]={\mathcal F}$ as $\theta^{-n}({\mathcal F}) \ge {\mathcal F}$. 
Thus $\tilde{{\mathcal F}} \ge {\mathcal F}$. So $\tilde{{\mathcal F}} \ge \tilde{\Lambda}^n({\mathcal F})$ for all $n \ge 1$ and taking limit we get $\tilde{{\mathcal F}} \ge I$ i.e. $\tilde{{\mathcal F}}=I$. 
This contradicts our starting assumption that $\tilde{{\mathcal F}}$ is a proper projection.  

\vskip 1em 
\noindent {\bf Sub-case 2 of case 2:} Now we consider the case $G=\tilde{{\mathcal F}} < I$. In such a case we have 
$(1- \tilde{{\mathcal F}})\theta^{-n}({\mathcal F})\tilde{{\mathcal F}}=0$ and so $\theta^{-n}({\mathcal F})$ commutes with $\tilde{{\mathcal F}}$ for all $n \ge 0$. 

\vskip 1em 
First we rule out the simplest possibility in the present situation for ${\mathcal F} \tilde{{\mathcal F}} = |\Omega><\Omega|$. If so then $\omega$ is
a Bernoulli state and a proof follows once we compute the following using the property $\Lambda(\tilde{{\mathcal F}}) \ge \tilde{{\mathcal F}}$ i.e.
$\tilde{{\mathcal F}}\pi(s_i)^*\tilde{{\mathcal F}} = \pi(s_i)^*\tilde{{\mathcal F}}$ 
and commuting property of ${\mathcal F}$ with $\pi(s_i)^*$ to get some scalars $\bar{\lambda_i}$ such
that 
$$\bar{\lambda}_i= {\mathcal F}\tilde{{\mathcal F}}\pi(s_i)^*\tilde{{\mathcal F}}{\mathcal F} = \pi(s_i)^*\tilde{{\mathcal F}}{\mathcal F}$$
and so 
$$\omega(s_Is_J^*)=<\Omega,\pi(s_I) \pi(s_J)^*\Omega>$$
$$=<\Omega, {\mathcal F} \tilde{{\mathcal F}} \pi(s_I)\pi(s_J)^*\tilde{{\mathcal F}}{\mathcal F} \Omega>$$
$$=\lambda_I\lambda_J^*$$
The inductive limit state $\omega$ on ${\mathcal B}$, give rises to a pure state once restricted to ${\mathcal B}_R$ and thus we have 
${\mathcal E}=\tilde{{\mathcal F}}$ by Haag duality when $\pi({\mathcal B}_R)''$ is a type-I factor. This contradicts our starting assumption that ${\mathcal E}=I$.   

\vskip 1em 
Now we set projection ${\mathcal F}'$ defined by 
\begin{equation} 
{\mathcal F}'={\mathcal F}-{\mathcal F}\tilde{{\mathcal F}}+|\Omega><\Omega|
\end{equation} 
and check by commuting property of $\tilde{{\mathcal F}}$ with ${\mathcal F}$ that 
$$ 
{\mathcal F}'\theta^{-1}({\mathcal F}'){\mathcal F}' = (I-\tilde{{\mathcal F}}){\mathcal F}\theta^{-1}({\mathcal F})(I-\theta^{-1}(\tilde{{\mathcal F}}))(I-\tilde{{\mathcal F}}){\mathcal F} 
+ |\Omega><\Omega|$$ 
$$= {\mathcal F}(I-\tilde{{\mathcal F}}) + |\Omega><\Omega|={\mathcal F}'$$ 
where we have used $\theta^{-1}({\mathcal F}) = \tilde{\Lambda}({\mathcal F}) \ge {\mathcal F},\; \theta({\mathcal F}) \le {\mathcal F}$ and  
$\theta(\tilde{{\mathcal F}}) = \Lambda(\tilde{{\mathcal F}}) \ge \tilde{{\mathcal F}}$. 
Thus we get 
\begin{equation} 
\theta^{-1}({\mathcal F}') \ge {\mathcal F}'
\end{equation}                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     

\vskip 1em 
We also rule out the possibility that ${\mathcal F} \tilde{{\mathcal F}} = {\mathcal F}$. If so then ${\mathcal F} \le \tilde{{\mathcal F}}$ and $\tilde{\Lambda}^n({\mathcal F}) \le 
\tilde{\Lambda}^n(\tilde{{\mathcal F}}) = \tilde{{\mathcal F}}$. Taking limit we get $\tilde{{\mathcal F}}=I$ as $\tilde{\Lambda}^n({\mathcal F}) \uparrow I$ as $n \rightarrow \infty$. 
This brings a contradiction to our hypothesis.  
  
\vskip 1em 
So we have in particular ${\mathcal F}' <  {\mathcal F} \le I$ and ${\mathcal F}' - |\Omega><\Omega| \neq 0$. Now we will rule out the possibility of ${\mathcal F}=I$ under our hypothesis $\tilde{{\mathcal F}} < {\mathcal E}=I$. 
Suppose so i.e. ${\mathcal F}=I$, then $\tilde{{\mathcal E}}=I$ since $\tilde{{\mathcal E}} \ge {\mathcal F}$. Then $Q={\mathcal E} \tilde{{\mathcal E}} = {\mathcal E} = {\mathcal E} {\mathcal F}=P$. Thus by Proposition 3.5 (e) we get $\pi({\mathcal O}_d)'= 
\pi(\tilde{{\mathcal O}}_d)''$ and so we have in particular $\tilde{{\mathcal F}}=[\pi(\tilde{{\mathcal O}}_d)''\Omega]=[\pi({\mathcal O}_d)'\Omega]={\mathcal E}$. This contradicts our starting assumption once more that $\tilde{{\mathcal F}} < {\mathcal E}=I$.    

\vskip 1em 
We also have $\theta^{-1}({\mathcal F}') \ge {\mathcal F}'$ and $\theta^{-1}({\mathcal F}) \ge {\mathcal F}$. Thus we can follow the steps of Case-1 with elements ${\mathcal F}',{\mathcal F},\theta^{-1}$ replacing the role of $\tilde{{\mathcal F}},{\mathcal E},\theta$ 
to get a unitary operator $U:nH \rightarrow nH$ so that $U\bar{V}=\bar{V}U$ and $U\bar{{\mathcal F}}U^*=\bar{{\mathcal F}'}$ for a 
cardinal number $n$.    

\vskip 1em 
Now we consider a further subset ${\mathcal P}_{G'}$ of ${\mathcal P}_G$ consist of quasi-equivalent representations $\pi$ to $\pi_0$ 
of ${\mathcal B}$ where $\pi$ admits the additional property: ${\mathcal F}_{\pi} < I, {\mathcal E}_{\pi}=I$ and $\{\theta^{-n}(\tilde{{\mathcal F}_{\pi}}): n \ge 0 \}$ 
commutes with ${\mathcal F}_{\pi}$ with the strict partial ordering $({\mathcal H}_{\pi_1},\pi_1,\Omega_{\pi_1}) \prec ({\mathcal H}_{\pi_2},\pi_2,\Omega_{\pi_2})$ 
given by modifying condition (C3') as

\vskip 1em 
\noindent (C3'') $\oplus_{1 \le \alpha \le n_{\pi_1} }[\pi^{\alpha}_1(\mbox{UHF}_d)''\Omega^1_{\alpha}] >  \oplus_{1 \le 
\alpha \le n_{\pi_2}}[\pi^{\alpha}_2(\mbox{UHF}_d)''\Omega^2_{\alpha}]E'_2$

\vskip 1em 
Since $\pi^U$ also satisfies the conditions that of $\pi_0 \in {\mathcal P}_{G'}$ by covariance relation 
of $U$ with respect to shifts once more we get $\pi^U \in {\mathcal P}_{G'}$ and $\pi_0 \prec \pi^U$. Thus we can 
repeat the process and so ${\mathcal P}_{G'}$ has at least one infinite chain of totally ordered containing $\pi_0$.   
Once more by Hausdorff maximality principle we bring a contradiction to our starting assumption 
that ${\mathcal F}' < {\mathcal F}$. In other words this brings a contradiction to our starting hypothesis 
that $\tilde{{\mathcal F}}$ is a proper projection i.e. ${\mathcal F} < {\mathcal E}=I$. Thus we arrive at $\tilde{{\mathcal F}}={\mathcal E}$ 
when ${\mathcal E}=I$. 

\vskip 1em 
By symmetry of argument used here it also follows that ${\mathcal F}=\tilde{{\mathcal E}}$ when $\tilde{{\mathcal E}}=I$. This completes the proof of 
$\tilde{{\mathcal F}}={\mathcal E},\;\; {\mathcal F} =\tilde{{\mathcal E}}$ for the case when $H$ is the trivial closed subgroup of $S^1$. 

\vskip 1em 
Now we will remove the assumption that $H$ is trivial using Proposition 3.4. Let $(H,\pi_0,\Omega)$ be the GNS space of the state $\omega$ on ${\mathcal B}$. 
Let $e_0$ and $\tilde{e}_0$ be the support projections of $\omega$ in $\pi_0({\mathcal B}_R)''$ and $\pi_0({\mathcal B}_L)''$ respectively. Similarly we also 
set projections ${\mathcal F}_0=[\pi_0({\mathcal A}_R)''\Omega]$ and $\tilde{{\mathcal F}}_0=[\pi_0({\mathcal B}_L)''\Omega]$. We also set projections 
$q_0=[\pi_0(\mbox{UHF})'\Omega] [\pi_0(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d)'\Omega]$ and $p_0=[\pi_0(\mbox{UHF})'\Omega] [\pi_0(\mbox{UHF}_d)''\Omega]$.  


\vskip 1em 
$\omega$ being pure, by Theorem 3.4 any $\{\beta_z:z \in H \}$ invariant element of ${\mathcal B}(\tilde{{\mathcal H}} \otimes_{{\mathcal K}} {\mathcal H})$ is an element in 
$\pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d)''$. ${\mathcal E},\tilde{{\mathcal E}},{\mathcal F}, \tilde{{\mathcal F}}$ are $\{\beta_z:z \in H \}$ elements. Thus once 
we identify cyclic space $[\pi_0({\mathcal B})\Omega]$ with $F_0=[\pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d)''\Omega]$, we get obvious relations 
\begin{equation} 
{\mathcal E} F_0=e_0,\tilde{{\mathcal E}}F_0=\tilde{e}_0,{\mathcal F} F_0=f_0, \tilde{{\mathcal F}}F_0=\tilde{f}_0
\end{equation}
and 
\begin{equation} 
P F_0 = p_0 \;\;\mbox{and} \;\; QF_0=q_0
\end{equation}
as 
${\mathcal E}=[\pi(\mbox{UHF})'\Omega]$, $\tilde{{\mathcal E}} = [\pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d)'\Omega]$, $Q={\mathcal E}\tilde{{\mathcal E}}$ and $P={\mathcal E} {\mathcal F}$. Further $V$ is also 
$\{ \beta_z:z \in H \}$ invariant and $V \pi(x)V^*=\pi(\theta(x))$ for all $x \in {\mathcal B}$ which we have identified with $\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d$. 

\vskip 1em 
By applying the first part of the argument with representation $\pi_0$, for pure $\omega$, we have 
$e_0=\tilde{f}_0$ and $\tilde{e}_0=f_0$ and $p_0=q_0$.  


\vskip 1em 
Now we write the equality $p_0=q_0$ as ${\mathcal E} {\mathcal F} F_0={\mathcal E}\tilde{{\mathcal E}}F_0$ and apply $\Lambda$ on both side to
